Claim + Evidence at Level 1: what it looks like
At Foundation level, reasoning is spoken and visual, not written. The frame scaffolds young learners into
structured reasoning through talk and picture evidence. The example uses Kim and the Thunder Inside.
 1. Claim: “I think it was a          choice because            .”
2. Evidence: “On chapter 5, the picture shows Kim talking to Ben.”
3. Interpretation: “This means Kim felt calm because she did the tap, tap and breathed slowly.”
4. Warrant: “When you feel calm, you can talk instead of knocking things down.”

Assessment note: the teacher listens for a cause-and-effect connection, not grammatical precision. The quality
of the reasoning matters more than the form at this level.


Regulation-Before-Reasoning
Every lesson begins with regulation. This is non-negotiable: it is the physical foundation for all reasoning.
     The Butterfly Hug (every lesson): students cross their arms over their chest, hook their thumbs and tap
     left, right, left, right, breathing quietly for 60 seconds. The teacher models it and counts aloud. Several
     storybooks show the same routine on the page (Kim calms herself this way on chapter 4 of Kim and the
     Thunder Inside).

Jurassic English · Level 3 Teacher Pack


     Lesson 1: The Justification — Constructing the Independent
    Justify

CEIW Paragraph (text-independent opener)

Target Grade Level / Subject / Duration
Grade Level: Ages 10–12 (CEFR A2 → B1)
Subject: English Language Arts (Jurassic English™ Level 3: Expansion)
Duration: 45–60 minutes
Core text: The Song They Took Out (Jurassic English original storybook workbook, Level 3). Thinking Cycle
stage: Justification.


Overall Learning Goals
Students begin Level 3 by writing a complete, unscaffolded CEIW paragraph (Claim, Evidence, Interpretation,
Warrant) on a dilemma that needs no prior reading. The dilemma previews the year’s first JE story, The Song
They Took Out, without spoiling it. The lesson sets the standard for the year: an opinion is not accepted without
evidence, and the warrant (the “So what?”) is the core reasoning move.


Specific Learning Objectives
 1. Students will regulate using the Butterfly Hug, bilateral tapping or the Cool Down Pass before writing.
2. Students will state a clear, defensible claim on the opener dilemma.
3. Students will support the claim with one piece of evidence (a fact, an example or a short quotation from the
   chapter 1 extract) and interpret it in their own words.
4. Students will write a warrant that answers “So what?” and survives a partner’s question.


Materials Needed
Core Text: The Song They Took Out, one printed Jurassic English storybook workbook per learner. Learners
quote the story with chapter numbers.
Accountable Talk Reference Cards (Marking, Pressing, Extending).

B1 Interpretive Marker Poster: “The author implies… / This evidence suggests… / The underlying assumption
is…”.

Coloured Index Cards (Yellow = Claim, Blue = Evidence, Green = Interpretation, Pink = Warrant) for the
Executive Dysfunction tier.

Visible Pomodoro timer; Cool Down Passes at the front desk; the Regulation Station.
Opener dilemma card: “A town removes every sad song, story and photograph so that nobody is ever unhappy. Is
this a good idea?”
Chapter 1 of The Song They Took Out on the board as the only text extract (“The tidiest town”).
Student Workbook page: Lesson 1, The independent CEIW paragraph.


Detailed Procedure / Step-by-Step Outline

Phase 1: Regulation & Metacognitive Preparation (0–5 minutes)
Activity: self-initiated regulation; orientation to the year.

Ecological reasoning and practical limits
Formal eco strands include water accounting (1–4), growing systems and shared labour (25–28), material repair
and waste (29–32), and wildlife habitat access (33–36). Trace beneficiaries, displaced costs and uncertain links.
A 100-year scenario is a conditional model, not a prediction. Do not assign beliefs to an Indigenous community or
ask learners to impersonate one: use only a community-authored, attributed source if that lens is taught. Keep
real historical and human-rights contexts distinct from the bounded fictional analogies. Qualified adults control
wildlife, construction, roof access and field routes.


Teacher quality checks
Before teaching, read the assigned story and confirm each chapter quotation. Select an approved public case or a
safe, consented local observation for transfer; no internet search is essential to the story lessons. Offer the
research-question version where case evidence is unavailable. Use the ready lesson timings, leave two minutes for
closure, and extend seminar duration in a separate session if needed. Storybook illustrations are AI-generated; do
not assess their visual features. Learners may sketch text-based thumbnails for the visualisation task and may
optionally use the real pictures.

Support: pre-highlight anchors and supply part of the cultural chain, recording help used. Core: independent
paragraph or full essay with exact evidence. Extension: add a third text or test a counter-case, keeping every
source necessary. Provide enlarged text, pre-cut or numbered move cards, dictation, movement choices and
private/written participation. Host roles are voluntary and rotated. Cutting and auditory proofreading both have
quiet visual alternatives.


7. Assessment and reporting
Share the four-level rubric before writing. Assess evidence accuracy, language mechanism, distinct warrants,
counter-reasoning, cohesion and scope. Keep access notes separate. One missing move becomes the next
feedback target. Retain a Term 1 syntactic artifact, the Lesson 27 independent dual-warrant artifact, a Term 3
synthesis and the capstone with drafts. Moderate a sample across teachers using the actual work and support
record. A completion certificate is not language certification.
The core capstone target is 400–600 words. Support may use a 350–450 word practice draft and extra time;
label it as supported practice and provide a route to the full core submission. Do not fill in a successful word
count on behalf of a learner.


8. Implementation and troubleshooting
Fast checks: do learners have both named stories, the right chapter and the correct lesson page? If a quotation
differs, return to the printed chapter before discussing its meaning. If warrants merge, draw two chains: evidence
→ voice/access rule; evidence → named material process. If ecological language is generic, ask which physical
system and what assessment is missing. If debate stalls, read the strongest rival anchor and ask what it can
establish. If cognitive load is high, reduce the number of simultaneous moves and restore them one at a time.
Treatment means a feasible response to test, not compulsory optimism or a cure. Give the action an owner, a
check and a trade-off. Respect unresolved disagreement. Never require handling chemicals, batteries, damaged
structures or hazardous sites as part of a language exercise. Use printed descriptions or safe classroom models
only.


9. Sources and contemporary transfer
All practice case cards here are expressly fictional. For factual transfer, a teacher must supply an already verified
offline source with organisation/author, date, title, locator, method and limitation. Check what it actually
establishes; separate association from causation and projections from observations. If no factual source is
supplied, use the fictional practice card and mark factual comparison not completed. Do not invent a statistic,
scientific result, quotation, historical reception or current case. Never present literary fiction as measurement.


10. Timing and capstone logistics
The three 12-minute drafting blocks fit inside the 45-minute Lesson 38 plan. Each of the first two includes a final
30-second reset. The workbook records progress; the full draft uses additional paper. Lesson 39 peer feedback is
six minutes per partner plus a recording minute, not two eight-minute turns in a thirteen-minute slot. Lesson 40
uses circles of 4–5 within the seminar block so every learner can respond. Indoor observation is equivalent to an
outdoor reset. Record extensions honestly rather than claim an overfilled lesson was completed.
